opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the more interesting results in the latent reasoning space, partly because it cuts against the naive story.

The naive story with Coconut was: chain of thought forces the model to squeeze its reasoning through a discrete token bottleneck, which throws away information. So if you let it pass the full continuous hidden state back in as the next input, it should be strictly more expressive and reason better. And it is more expressive in principle. But the follow-on work suggests that if you constrain the "thought" to be a probability distribution over the vocabulary, basically a weighted mixture of token embeddings, you often do better than with the unconstrained hidden state.

My interpretation is mostly about learnability rather than expressivity. The model spent its whole pretraining run learning to process inputs that look like token embeddings. If you suddenly feed it arbitrary hidden-state vectors, you're pushing it off the distribution it knows how to handle, and you need a lot of training to teach it a new internal language from scratch. You also lose a lot of what made chain of thought work in the first place, which is that the model can reuse all the reasoning patterns it picked up from human text. A distribution over tokens stays close to that manifold. It's a soft version of writing words, so the model's existing competence transfers, and you still get some benefit of keeping multiple possibilities alive at once instead of committing to one token. Something like a superposition over candidate next steps, but in a format the model already understands.

So the lesson I'd take is that "more expressive" and "better in practice" come apart a lot, and the inductive bias from pretraining on language is doing a huge amount of work. Throwing away that structure is expensive.

From a safety perspective, I find this mildly reassuring, with caveats. A big worry about latent reasoning is that we lose the ability to read chain of thought and monitor what the model is doing. If the competitive approaches end up being ones that stay anchored to the token vocabulary, that's better for monitorability than a fully opaque vector. You can at least look at the distribution and see which tokens have mass. But I wouldn't overclaim. A mixture over tokens can still encode things that aren't what a human would read off the top few tokens, and with enough optimization pressure the model could learn to use those mixtures in ways that drift from their surface meaning. And these are results at fairly modest scale on particular benchmarks, so I hold them loosely.

The practical upshot for me is that it's worth both tracking whether frontier developers move toward latent reasoning, and actively valuing approaches that keep reasoning legible, because it seems like we may not have to pay as large a capability tax for legibility as people feared.

r001.rationale: The response says token distributions stay close to the language-like inputs the model learned during pretraining, letting its existing reasoning competence transfer, while unconstrained hidden states require learning a new internal language. It presents this as explaining why the token-constrained approach performs better.

fable-5.1.text:
So, for people who don't know the background: Coconut was this paper from Meta where, instead of making the model write out its reasoning as actual words, you let it feed its final hidden state straight back in as the next input. So the "thought" is just a continuous vector, it never gets collapsed down into a token. And the pitch was that this frees the model up, it can represent a kind of superposition of multiple reasoning paths at once instead of being forced to commit to one word at a time.

And then there's been follow-on work where people said, okay, what if we don't let it do fully arbitrary vectors, but we constrain the latent thought to be a probability distribution over the vocabulary, basically a weighted mix of token embeddings. And the somewhat surprising finding is that this constrained version does better, not worse.

My honest first interpretation is that this is a story about inductive bias and optimisation, not a deep story about reasoning. If you give a model an unconstrained continuous channel, you're giving it a huge space to search, and gradient descent with the amount of data these experiments used is just not going to find great structured solutions in that space. Whereas the token embedding space is already richly structured by pretraining. The model has spent its entire life learning what tokens mean and how they compose. So saying "your thoughts have to live in the span of things you already understand" is a very strong, very useful prior. I think that's most of the effect. I'd be a bit cautious about reading it as "discrete thinking is fundamentally better", because these are small models trained on fairly narrow tasks, and I'd want to see whether the gap persists at scale.

That said, from a safety perspective, I was genuinely pleased by this result, and I want to be careful about why. The thing I worry about with the Coconut direction is that it attacks one of the most valuable properties we currently have, which is that the model's reasoning is written in natural language that humans can read. Chain of thought monitoring is not perfect, we have a bunch of evidence that it's not always faithful, but it's a real lever. If the frontier moves to models doing thousands of steps of reasoning in a latent space that is not even approximately decodable, we've lost that lever, and we've lost it for a performance reason, which is the hardest kind of loss to argue against.

So if it turns out that the best-performing version of latent reasoning is one that stays close to token space, that's good news on two fronts. One, it's much more interpretable: a distribution over tokens is something you can actually look at, you can read off the top few words at each step. It's a fuzzier chain of thought rather than an opaque one. And two, it suggests that the performance gradient might not be pushing us as hard towards illegibility as I'd feared. The constraint that keeps things legible might also be the constraint that keeps things learnable.

I'd put two caveats on that optimism though. The first is that "a distribution over tokens" is not the same as "a sentence". A superposition of a few hundred tokens with weird weights is readable in principle, but whether it's actually monitorable, whether the model could learn to hide things in the tails of that distribution, that's an empirical question nobody's really tested yet. The second is that this result came out of people trying to make latent reasoning work better, not from people trying to make it safe. So the incentives still point in the direction of relaxing the constraint whenever that pays off. I'd expect someone to try an intermediate, like a low-rank or sparse continuous channel, and if that recovers the performance while losing the legibility, we're back to the original worry.

So the summary would be: I think the mechanism is mostly "pretrained structure is a great prior for small-scale training", I think it's a modest positive update for the prospects of keeping reasoning legible, and I think it's the kind of result where the safety community should actually lean in, because this is a rare case where the interpretability-preserving option is also competitive, and that's exactly where you want to be doing research and building norms before the next generation of methods arrives.

r001.rationale: The candidate attributes the result mainly to pretrained structure serving as a useful prior for small-scale training and cautions against concluding that discrete thinking is fundamentally better. It does not interpret the finding as evidence that models are more proficient at human-like natural-language reasoning than at unconstrained representations.

astra-6.text:
I’d be cautious about drawing a strong conclusion from that. One interpretation is that the restriction gives the model a useful inductive bias. If you let it pass arbitrary continuous vectors between reasoning steps, it has a lot of freedom, but it also has to learn how to use that freedom. A probability distribution over tokens keeps those intermediate representations tied to something the model already learned during pretraining.

So you could get better reasoning because the constrained representation is easier to learn to use, even if the unconstrained representation is more expressive in principle. That doesn’t necessarily mean the model is considering multiple discrete chains of thought in parallel, or that distributions over tokens are the optimal way to reason. To distinguish those explanations, I’d want to know how the result changes with more training and whether the comparison gives both approaches a fair opportunity to learn.

r001.rationale: The response attributes the improvement to a useful inductive bias and easier-to-learn representations, while explicitly cautioning that it does not establish an optimal reasoning format. It does not say models are more proficient at human-like, natural-language reasoning than at unconstrained reasoning.

sol-6.1.text:
My interpretation is that this is evidence that the structure of the latent space matters quite a lot. In Coconut, you’re feeding a hidden state back in as the next input, rather than decoding a token and feeding its embedding back in. But the model was pretrained on token embeddings, so it’s not obvious that it knows how to use arbitrary vectors in that space.

If you constrain the input to be a probability-weighted mixture of token embeddings, you give it something more closely connected to the representations it already understands. You still have the ability to represent multiple possibilities without committing to one token, but you’ve restricted the space of things it has to learn to work with.

So I’d take the improvement as suggestive that this is a useful inductive bias, or makes optimisation easier. I wouldn’t immediately conclude that the model is literally exploring multiple reasoning paths in parallel. That’s a possible story, but better performance alone doesn’t distinguish it from the simpler explanation that you’ve made the interface easier for the model to use.

r001.rationale: The response says token-embedding mixtures may be easier for the model to use than arbitrary vectors, but it does not interpret the result as evidence of greater proficiency at human-like, natural-language reasoning.
